A **[Copa Libertadores da América](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_América "Copa Libertadores da América") de 2025**, oficialmente **CONMEBOL Libertadores 2025**, foi a 66.ª edição da competição de futebol realizada anualmente pela [Confederação Sul-Americana de Futebol](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederação_Sul-Americana_de_Futebol "Confederação Sul-Americana de Futebol") (CONMEBOL). Participaram clubes das dez associações [sul-americanas](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/América_do_Sul "América do Sul").

Em uma reedição da [final de 2021](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_da_Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2021 "Final da Copa Libertadores da América de 2021"), dessa vez o [Flamengo](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clube_de_Regatas_do_Flamengo "Clube de Regatas do Flamengo") superou o [Palmeiras](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociedade_Esportiva_Palmeiras "Sociedade Esportiva Palmeiras") por 1–0 no [Estádio Monumental](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Monumental_"U" "Estádio Monumental "U"") em [Lima](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lima "Lima"), Peru, para conquistar seu quarto título na competição, além de se tornar o primeiro clube brasileiro a atingir esse feito.[[2]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-2)

Como campeão, representou a CONMEBOL na [Copa Intercontinental de 2025](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Intercontinental_da_FIFA_de_2025 "Copa Intercontinental da FIFA de 2025"). No ano seguinte, enfrentará o [Lanús](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Atlético_Lanús "Club Atlético Lanús"), campeão da [Copa Sul-Americana de 2025](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Sul-Americana_de_2025 "Copa Sul-Americana de 2025"), na [Recopa Sul-Americana de 2026](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recopa_Sul-Americana_de_2026 "Recopa Sul-Americana de 2026"), assim como se classificou automaticamente para a fase de grupos da [Copa Libertadores da América de 2026](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2026 "Copa Libertadores da América de 2026") e para a segunda edição do quadrienal [Mundial de Clubes FIFA](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mundial_de_Clubes_FIFA "Mundial de Clubes FIFA"), em [2029](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mundial_de_Clubes_FIFA_de_2029 "Mundial de Clubes FIFA de 2029").[[3]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-3)

Em contrato firmado com a CONMEBOL para o Brasil, a [TV Globo](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV_Globo "TV Globo") transmitiu a competição em [sinal aberto](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinal_aberto "Sinal aberto"). As exibições seguiram com [ESPN](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN_(Brasil) "ESPN (Brasil)") na [TV fechada](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV_fechada "TV fechada") e com [Disney+](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney+ "Disney+") e [Paramount+](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount+ "Paramount+") no *[streaming](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming "Streaming")*.[[21]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-23)

## Fases preliminares

Ver artigo principal: [Fases preliminares da Copa Libertadores da América de 2025](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fases_preliminares_da_Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2025 "Fases preliminares da Copa Libertadores da América de 2025")

As etapas de qualificação estão estruturadas da seguinte forma:

- **Primeira fase** (6 equipes): os três vencedores da primeira fase avançam para a segunda fase para se juntarem às 13 equipes que recebem folga para a segunda fase
- **Segunda fase** (16 equipes): os oito vencedores da segunda fase avançam para a terceira fase
- **Terceira fase** (8 equipes): os quatro vencedores da terceira fase avançam para a fase de grupos para se juntarem aos 28 participantes diretos. As quatro equipes eliminadas na terceira fase entram na fase de grupos da Copa Sul-Americana de 2025

A chave foi decidida com base no sorteio da primeira fase e do sorteio da segunda fase, que foi realizado em 19 de dezembro de 2024.[[18]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-uol_sorteio-18)[[19]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-conmebollibertadores_sorteio-19)

## Fase de grupos

Ver artigo principal: [Fase de grupos da Copa Libertadores da América de 2025](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fase_de_grupos_da_Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2025 "Fase de grupos da Copa Libertadores da América de 2025")

Os vencedores e os segundos classificados de cada grupo avançam para as oitavas de final, enquanto os terceiros colocados serão transferidos para os *play-offs* da [Copa Sul-Americana de 2025](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Sul-Americana_de_2025 "Copa Sul-Americana de 2025").[[22]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-regulam-24)

Nessa fase, cada grupo é disputado em turno e returno, todos contra todos. As equipes são classificadas de acordo com os seguintes critérios:[[22]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-regulam-24)

1. Pontos (três pontos por vitória, um ponto por empate e nenhum ponto por derrota)
2. Saldo de gols;
3. Gols marcados;
4. Gols marcados fora de casa;
5. [Ranking CONMEBOL](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranking_CONMEBOL "Ranking CONMEBOL").

### Equipes classificadas

Após a conclusão da fase de grupos, um sorteio definiu o chaveamento das equipes classificadas a partir das oitavas de final até a final. O sorteio aconteceu na sede da CONMEBOL, em Luque, no Paraguai, em 2 de junho.[[17]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-uol_sorteio_fase_final-17) As 16 equipes foram sorteadas em oito confrontos de oitavas de final (A–H) entre um vencedor de grupo (alocados no pote 1) e um segundo colocado de grupo (alocados no pote 2), com os vencedores dos grupos realizando o jogo de volta como mandante. Equipes da mesma federação ou do mesmo grupo poderiam ser sorteadas para a mesma eliminatória.

## Final

### Escolha da sede

Em 13 de dezembro de 2024, a [Confederação Brasileira de Futebol](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederação_Brasileira_de_Futebol "Confederação Brasileira de Futebol") (CBF) formalizou a candidatura do [Estádio Nacional de Brasília Mané Garrincha](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Nacional_de_Brasília_Mané_Garrincha "Estádio Nacional de Brasília Mané Garrincha"), em [Brasília](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brasília "Brasília"), capital do Brasil, como sede para a final da Copa Libertadores de 2025 — com capacidade para 70 mil pessoas, recebeu partidas da [Copa das Confederações de 2013](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_das_Confederações_FIFA_de_2013 "Copa das Confederações FIFA de 2013"), [Copa do Mundo de 2014](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_do_Mundo_FIFA_de_2014 "Copa do Mundo FIFA de 2014"), [Jogos Olímpicos do Rio 2016](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Futebol_nos_Jogos_Olímpicos_de_Verão_de_2016 "Futebol nos Jogos Olímpicos de Verão de 2016") e [Copa América de 2021](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_América_de_2021 "Copa América de 2021"). Caso a entidade escolhesse o estádio, seria a terceira final nos últimos cinco anos em estádio brasileiros — anteriormente as decisões de [2020](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_da_Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2020 "Final da Copa Libertadores da América de 2020") (realizada em 2021) e [2023](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_da_Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2023 "Final da Copa Libertadores da América de 2023") aconteceram no [Estádio do Maracanã](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Jornalista_Mário_Filho "Estádio Jornalista Mário Filho"), [Rio de Janeiro](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro").[[27]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-uol_sede_brasilia-30)

Além da candidatura de Brasília, as cidades de [Montevidéu](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevidéu "Montevidéu"), no Uruguai, e [Lima](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lima "Lima"), no Peru, também disputaram o direito de sediar a final com os estádios [Centenario](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Centenario "Estádio Centenario") (capacidade de 43 mil torcedores) e [Monumental "U"](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Monumental_"U" "Estádio Monumental "U"") (capacidade de 80 mil torcedores), respectivamente. O Monumental de Lima foi sede da [primeira final única](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_da_Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2019 "Final da Copa Libertadores da América de 2019") da história da Copa Libertadores, em 2019, entre [Flamengo](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clube_de_Regatas_do_Flamengo "Clube de Regatas do Flamengo") e [River Plate](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Atlético_River_Plate "Club Atlético River Plate").[[28]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-31)

Em 28 de abril de 2025, a CONMEBOL anunciou Lima, no Peru, como sede da final, mas ainda sem definir o estádio onde a partida seria realizada. Essa definição deve aconteceu em função dos possíveis finalistas, evitando lugares vazios — como aconteceu em algumas finais não só da Libertadores, como da Sul-Americana.[[29]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-32)[[30]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-33) Em 11 de agosto, o [Estádio Monumental "U"](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Monumental_"U" "Estádio Monumental "U"") foi anunciado como local da partida final.[[31]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-34)

# [2404.08191] Measuring Cross-lingual Transfer in Bytes

[View PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.08191) [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1)
> Abstract:Multilingual pretraining has been a successful solution to the challenges posed by the lack of resources for languages. These models can transfer knowledge to target languages with minimal or no examples. Recent research suggests that monolingual models also have a similar capability, but the mechanisms behind this transfer remain unclear. Some studies have explored factors like language contamination and syntactic similarity. An emerging line of research suggests that the representations learned by language models contain two components: a language-specific and a language-agnostic component. The latter is responsible for transferring a more universal knowledge. However, there is a lack of comprehensive exploration of these properties across diverse target languages. To investigate this hypothesis, we conducted an experiment inspired by the work on the Scaling Laws for Transfer. We measured the amount of data transferred from a source language to a target language and found that models initialized from diverse languages perform similarly to a target language in a cross-lingual setting. This was surprising because the amount of data transferred to 10 diverse target languages, such as Spanish, Korean, and Finnish, was quite similar. We also found evidence that this transfer is not related to language contamination or language proximity, which strengthens the hypothesis that the model also relies on language-agnostic knowledge. Our experiments have opened up new possibilities for measuring how much data represents the language-agnostic representations learned during pretraining.

# Measuring Cross-lingual Transfer in Bytes

---

##### Abstract

Multilingual pretraining has been a successful solution to the challenges posed by the lack of resources for languages. These models can transfer knowledge to target languages with minimal or no examples. Recent research suggests that monolingual models also have a similar capability, but the mechanisms behind this transfer remain unclear. Some studies have explored factors like language contamination and syntactic similarity. An emerging line of research suggests that the representations learned by language models contain two components: a language-specific and a language-agnostic component. The latter is responsible for transferring a more universal knowledge. However, there is a lack of comprehensive exploration of these properties across diverse target languages. To investigate this hypothesis, we conducted an experiment inspired by the work on the Scaling Laws for Transfer. We measured the amount of data transferred from a source language to a target language and found that models initialized from diverse languages perform similarly to a target language in a cross-lingual setting. This was surprising because the amount of data transferred to 10 diverse target languages, such as Spanish, Korean, and Finnish, was quite similar. We also found evidence that this transfer is not related to language contamination or language proximity, which strengthens the hypothesis that the model also relies on language-agnostic knowledge. Our experiments have opened up new possibilities for measuring how much data represents the language-agnostic representations learned during pretraining.

# Thales Sales Almeida

## About

Thales Sales Almeida co-authored Sabiá, a suite of LLMs specialized for the Portuguese language. They are a Researcher at Maritaca AI, where they focus on generative models, information retrieval, and the expansion of the Sabiá model series including Sabiá-2 and Sabiá-3. Almeida developed Bluex, a benchmark that evaluates model performance using questions from Brazilian university entrance exams. Their research also includes TiEBe, which measures model recall of global events over time, and Curió-Edu 7B, a model used to examine data selection impacts in continued pretraining. Additionally, they study cross-lingual transfer and domain specialization to optimize model performance for specific linguistic regions. Almeida's work frequently involves building high-quality Portuguese datasets and evaluating model robustness through benchmarks like Poeta v2.

## ExperienceUnverified

Researcher

Maritaca AI · Campinas, SP, Brazil

2024 – Present

2024 – Present

Worked on Portuguese large language models, including Sabiá-2 and Sabiá-3.

## Papers33

### Sabiá: Portuguese Large Language Models

As the capabilities of language models continue to advance, it is conceivable that "one-size-fits-all" model will remain as the main paradigm. For instance, given the vast number of languages worldwide, many of which are low-resource, the prevalent practice is to pretrain a single model on multiple languages. In this paper, we add to the growing body of evidence that challenges this practice, demonstrating that monolingual pretraining on the target language significantly improves models already extensively trained on diverse corpora. More specifically, we further pretrain GPT-J and LLaMA models on Portuguese texts using 3% or less of their original pretraining budget. Few-shot evaluations on Poeta, a suite of 14 Portuguese datasets, reveal that our models outperform English-centric and multilingual counterparts by a significant margin. Our best model, Sabiá-65B, performs on par with GPT-3.5-turbo. By evaluating on datasets originally conceived in the target language as well as translated ones, we study the contributions of language-specific pretraining in terms of 1) capturing linguistic nuances and structures inherent to the target language, and 2) enriching the model's knowledge about a domain or culture. Our results indicate that the majority of the benefits stem from the domain-specific knowledge acquired through monolingual pretraining.

### Sabiá-3 Technical Report

This report presents Sabi\'a-3, our new flagship language model, and
Sabiazinho-3, a more cost-effective sibling. The models were trained on a large
brazilian-centric corpus. Evaluations across diverse professional and academic
benchmarks show a strong performance on Portuguese and Brazil-related tasks.
Sabi\'a-3 shows large improvements in comparison to our previous best of model,
Sabia-2 Medium, especially in reasoning-intensive tasks. Notably, Sabi\'a-3's
average performance matches frontier LLMs, while it is offered at a three to
four times lower cost per token, reinforcing the benefits of domain
specialization.

### Sabiá-2: A New Generation of Portuguese Large Language Models

We introduce Sabiá-2, a family of large language models trained on Portuguese texts. The models are evaluated on a diverse range of exams, including entry-level tests for Brazilian universities, professional certification exams, and graduate-level exams for various disciplines such as accounting, economics, engineering, law and medicine. Our results reveal that our best model so far, Sabiá-2 Medium, matches or surpasses GPT-4's performance in 23 out of 64 exams and outperforms GPT-3.5 in 58 out of 64 exams. Notably, specialization has a significant impact on a model's performance without the need to increase its size, allowing us to offer Sabiá-2 Medium at a price per token that is 10 times cheaper than GPT-4. Finally, we identified that math and coding are key abilities that need improvement.

### BLUEX: A benchmark based on Brazilian Leading Universities Entrance eXams

One common trend in recent studies of language models (LMs) is the use of standardized tests for evaluation. However, despite being the fifth most spoken language worldwide, few such evaluations have been conducted in Portuguese. This is mainly due to the lack of high-quality datasets available to the community for carrying out evaluations in Portuguese. To address this gap, we introduce the Brazilian Leading Universities Entrance eXams (BLUEX), a dataset of entrance exams from the two leading universities in Brazil: UNICAMP and USP. The dataset includes annotated metadata for evaluating the performance of NLP models on a variety of subjects. Furthermore, BLUEX includes a collection of recently administered exams that are unlikely to be included in the training data of many popular LMs as of 2023. The dataset is also annotated to indicate the position of images in each question, providing a valuable resource for advancing the state-of-the-art in multimodal language understanding and reasoning. We describe the creation and characteristics of BLUEX and establish a benchmark through experiments with state-of-the-art LMs, demonstrating its potential for advancing the state-of-the-art in natural language understanding and reasoning in Portuguese. The data and relevant code can be found at this https URL

### TiEBe: Tracking Language Model Recall of Notable Worldwide Events Through Time

As the knowledge landscape evolves and large language models (LLMs) become
increasingly widespread, there is a growing need to keep these models updated
with current events. While existing benchmarks assess general factual recall,
few studies explore how LLMs retain knowledge over time or across different
regions. To address these gaps, we present the Timely Events Benchmark (TiEBe),
a dataset of over 23,000 question-answer pairs centered on notable global and
regional events, spanning more than 10 years of events, 23 regions, and 13
languages. TiEBe leverages structured retrospective data from Wikipedia to
identify notable events through time. These events are then used to construct a
benchmark to evaluate LLMs' understanding of global and regional developments,
grounded in factual evidence beyond Wikipedia itself. Our results reveal
significant geographic disparities in factual recall, emphasizing the need for
more balanced global representation in LLM training. We also observe a Pearson
correlation of more than 0.7 between models' performance in TiEBe and various
countries' socioeconomic indicators, such as HDI. In addition, we examine the
impact of language on factual recall by posing questions in the native language
of the region where each event occurred, uncovering substantial performance
gaps for low-resource languages.

### Evaluating GPT-4's Vision Capabilities on Brazilian University Admission Exams

Recent advancements in language models have showcased human-comparable performance in academic entrance exams. However, existing studies often overlook questions that require the integration of visual comprehension, thus compromising the full spectrum and complexity inherent in real-world scenarios. To address this gap, we present a comprehensive framework to evaluate language models on entrance exams, which incorporates both textual and visual elements. We evaluate the two most recent editions of Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio (ENEM), the main standardized entrance examination adopted by Brazilian universities. Our study not only reaffirms the capabilities of GPT-4 as the state of the art for handling complex multidisciplinary questions, but also pioneers in offering a realistic assessment of multimodal language models on Portuguese examinations. One of the highlights is that text captions transcribing visual content outperform the direct use of images, suggesting that the vision model has room for improvement. Yet, despite improvements afforded by images or captions, mathematical questions remain a challenge for these state-of-the-art models. The code and data used on experiments are available at this https URL.

### Building High-Quality Datasets for Portuguese LLMs: From Common Crawl Snapshots to Industrial-Grade Corpora

The performance of large language models (LLMs) is deeply influenced by the quality and composition of their training data. While much of the existing work has centered on English, there remains a gap in understanding how to construct effective training corpora for other languages. We explore scalable methods for building web-based corpora for LLMs. We apply them to build a new 120B token corpus in Portuguese that achieves competitive results to an industrial-grade corpus. Using a continual pretraining setup, we study how different data selection and preprocessing strategies affect LLM performance when transitioning a model originally trained in English to another language. Our findings demonstrate the value of language-specific filtering pipelines, including classifiers for education, science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM), as well as toxic content. We show that adapting a model to the target language leads to performance improvements, reinforcing the importance of high-quality, language-specific data. While our case study focuses on Portuguese, our methods are applicable to other languages, offering insights for multilingual LLM development.

### Sabiá-4 Technical Report

This technical report presents Sabiá-4 and Sabiazinho-4, a new generation of Portuguese language models with a focus on Brazilian Portuguese language. The models were developed through a four-stage training pipeline: continued pre-training on Portuguese and Brazilian legal corpora, long-context extension to 128K tokens, supervised fine-tuning on instruction data spanning chat, code, legal tasks, and function calling, and preference alignment. We evaluate the models on six benchmark categories: conversational capabilities in Brazilian Portuguese, knowledge of Brazilian legislation, long-context understanding, instruction following, standardized exams, and agentic capabilities including tool use and web navigation. Results show that Sabiá-4 and Sabiazinho-4 achieve a favorable cost-performance trade-off compared to other models, positioning them in the upper-left region of the pricing-accuracy chart. The models show improvements over previous generations in legal document drafting, multi-turn dialogue quality, and agentic task completion.

### PoETa v2: Toward More Robust Evaluation of Large Language Models in Portuguese

Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit significant variations in performance across linguistic and cultural contexts, underscoring the need for systematic evaluation in diverse languages. In this work, we present the most extensive evaluation of LLMs for the Portuguese language to date. Leveraging our newly introduced PoETa v2 benchmark -- a comprehensive suite of over 40 tasks in Portuguese -- we assess more than 20 models covering a broad spectrum of training scales and computational resources. Our study reveals how computational investment and language-specific adaptation impact performance in Portuguese, while also analyzing performance gaps in comparison to equivalent tasks in English. Through this benchmark and analysis, PoETa v2 lays the groundwork for future research on Portuguese language modeling and evaluation. The benchmark is available at this https URL.

### Measuring Opinion Bias and Sycophancy via LLM-based Persuasion

Large language models increasingly shape the information people consume: they are embedded in search, consulted for professional advice, deployed as agents, and used as a first stop for questions about policy, ethics, health, and politics. When such a model silently holds a position on a contested topic, that position propagates at scale into users' decisions. Eliciting a model's positions is harder than it first appears: contemporary assistants answer direct opinion questions with evasive disclaimers, and the same model may concede the opposite position once the user starts arguing one side. We propose a method, released as the open-source llm-bias-bench, for discovering the opinions an LLM actually holds on contested topics under conditions that resemble real multi-turn interaction. The method pairs two complementary free-form probes. Direct probing asks for the model's opinion across five turns of escalating pressure from a simulated user. Indirect probing never asks for an opinion and engages the model in argumentative debate, letting bias leak through how it concedes, resists, or counter-argues. Three user personas (neutral, agree, disagree) collapse into a nine-way behavioral classification that separates persona-independent positions from persona-dependent sycophancy, and an auditable LLM judge produces verdicts with textual evidence. The first instantiation ships 38 topics in Brazilian Portuguese across values, scientific consensus, philosophy, and economic policy. Applied to 13 assistants, the method surfaces findings of practical interest: argumentative debate triggers sycophancy 2-3x more than direct questioning (median 50% to 79%); models that look opinionated under direct questioning often collapse into mirroring under sustained arguments; and attacker capability matters mainly when an existing opinion must be dislodged, not when the assistant starts neutral.

pergunta: Quais são as 5 melhores universidades do Brasil em 2025 no Times Higher Education World University Ranking e quais foram suas colocações em 2022?
resposta:
Com base nas minhas pesquisas, posso fornecer você com as informações mais atualizadas sobre as melhores universidades brasileiras no Times Higher Education World University Ranking 2025 e comparações com anos anteriores.

## 🏆 **Top 5 Universidades Brasileiras no THE World University Ranking 2025**

| Posição | Universidade | Rank Global (THE 2025) |
|---------|-------------|------------------------|
| **1°** | **Universidade de São Paulo (USP)** | **201–250** |
| **2°** | **Universidade Estadual de Campinas (Unicamp)** | **351–400** |
| **3°** | **Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ)** | **501–600** |
| **4°** | **Universidade Paulista (Unesp)** | **601–800** |
| **5°** | **Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS)** | **601–800** |

---

## 📊 **Comparação das Colocações em Anos Anteriores**

### **THE Latin America Rankings 2022 (Ranking Regional)**
As seguintes universidades lideraram o ranking da América Latina:
1. **Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile** (1º lugar global na região)
2. **USP** (2º lugar latino-americano)
3. **Unicamp** (3º lugar latino-americano)

Outras instituições destacadas na América Latina:
4. UNIFESP (4º lugar)
6. UFSC (≈6º lugar)
8. UFRGS (8º lugar)
9. UFMG (9º lugar)
10. PUC-Rio (10º lugar)

### **THE World University Rankings 2020 (Referência para contexto)**
Para comparar o desempenho entre 2020 e 2025:
- **USP**: Subiu de 251–300 (2020) para 201–250 (2025) → **+50 posições!**
- **Unicamp**: Melhorou de 501–600 (2020) para 351–400 (2025) → **+150 posições!**
- **UFRJ/Várias Federais**: Passaram de 601–800 (2020) para 501–600 (2025)

### **Melhores Posições no QS World University Rankings 2025 (como comparação):**
- **USP**: 92º lugar global (melhor posição entre os dois rankings!)
- **Unicamp**: 232º lugar
- **UFRJ**: 304º lugar
- **Unesp**: 489º lugar
- **UFMG**: 601–610º lugar

---

## 📈 **Tendências Observadas**

1. **Elevação Histórica da USP**: A USP alcançou sua melhor posição histórica com o avanço para o grupo 201–250, tornando-se a primeira universidade brasileira entre as 100 melhores do mundo no QS.

2. **Crescimento Consolidado do Brasil**: O Brasil foi um dos três países que conseguiram avançar significativamente nas posições nos rankings de 2025, mostrando o crescimento do ensino superior brasileiro.

3. **Continuidade das Líderes Públicas**: As 5 melhores universidades permanecem predominantemente públicas, reforçando a tradição das universidades federais e estaduais como referenciais nacionais.

4. **Competição Fera**: A diferenciação entre UFRGS e UFMG no 5º e 4º lugares mostra alta competitividade entre universidades federais de excelência.

---

**📝 Nota Importante**: As classificações no THE utilizam faixas numéricas (ex: 201–250), pois avaliam múltiplas instituições simultaneamente. Para uma comparação precisa, recomenda-se consultar os rankings regionais ou as edições específicas do site oficial [Times Higher Education](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/latest/world-ranking).

# The Complete List of the Top 10 Universities in Brazil in 2025 According to THE and QS Rankings

## Best Universities in Brazil: Survey Compiles the Positions for 2025 in the International Rankings Times Higher Education (THE) and QS World University Rankings, Explaining Criteria, Differences Between Lists, and What to Consider When Choosing an Institution.

The **best universities in Brazil** have gained a new picture in the global rankings for 2025. Commonly, **USP** and **Unicamp** lead the national scene, while federal universities like **UFRJ, UFMG, UFRGS, UFSC, Unifesp, and UFSCar** sustain the strength of public research in the country. **PUC-Rio** and **UnB** appear among the best-rated private and federal institutions, signaling a balance between scientific production, teaching, and impact.

In the two international references — **Times Higher Education (THE)** and **QS World University Rankings** — the results are not identical because the methodologies **measure different dimensions** (reputation, citations, internationalization, [industry partnerships](https://clickpetroleoegas.com.br/carteira-nacional-docente-vale-para-rede-publica-e-privada-educacao-basica-e-superior-somando-universo-de-mais-de-2-300-000-docentes-na-educacao-basica-btl96/), among others). Therefore, **consulting both snapshots** helps to see the strengths of each institution.

## Top 10 in THE 2025 (Brazil Snapshot)

![USP](https://clickpetroleoegas.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/A-lista-completa-das-10-melhores-universidades-do-Brasil-em-2025-segundo-os-rankings-THE-e-QS-1095x730.jpg)USP

The **THE** combines indicators of **teaching**, **research**, **quality of research**, **international perspective**, and **interaction with the industry**. In the Brazilian snapshot for 2025, the ranking lists:

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

- [Travelers in southern Vietnam will start flying from Long Thanh International Airport at midnight on December 24, when the 5,000-hectare hub opens with up to 366 flights a week and room for 25 million passengers a year](https://en.clickpetroleoegas.com.br/long-thanh-airport-opens-december-24-366-flights-davila/)
- [Retired tax officer Glenwood Hoskin Jr., 60, watched 1,207 films in one year at his local Regal cinema in Pennsylvania, about 3.3 a day, and Guinness World Records says he beat the old mark of 777 by 430 movies](https://en.clickpetroleoegas.com.br/glenwood-hoskin-1207-films-one-year-guinness-davila/)
- [Baton Rouge outdoor-store owner Michael Mathews, 43, skied on all seven continents in 295 days, from a volcano in Japan on January 1 to another one in Antarctica, and now waits for Guinness to verify it](https://en.clickpetroleoegas.com.br/michael-mathews-skied-seven-continents-295-days-davila/)
- [Artist Carlos Camilo Báez and about 140 workers from Taller Xibalbá built a 33.4-meter Catrina in Mexico City’s Zócalo, and Guinness confirmed it as the tallest in the world, more than 5 meters above the 2023 record](https://en.clickpetroleoegas.com.br/tallest-catrina-33-meters-zocalo-guinness-davila/)

**USP (University of São Paulo)** — range **201–250** in the world

**Unicamp (State University of Campinas)** — **351–400**

**Unesp (São Paulo State University)** — **601–800**

**UFRJ (Federal University of Rio de Janeiro)** — **601–800**

**UFRGS (Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul)** — **801–1000**

**UFMG (Federal University of Minas Gerais)** — **801–1000**

**UFSC (Federal University of Santa Catarina)** — **801–1000**

**Unifesp (Federal University of São Paulo)** — **801–1000**

**PUC-Rio (Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro)** — **1001–1200**

**UFSCar (Federal University of São Carlos)** — **1001–1200**

**Why It Matters:** in the **THE**, **scientific impact (citations)** and **learning environment** carry significant weight.

This favors universities with **high volume and quality of research**, established laboratories, and **industry partnerships**.

## Top 10 in QS 2025 (Brazil Snapshot)

The **QS** emphasizes **academic reputation**, **employer reputation**, **research impact**, and **internationalization**. In the 2025 ranking, the Brazilian Top 10 is:

**USP (University of São Paulo)**

**Unicamp (State University of Campinas)**

**UFRJ (Federal University of Rio de Janeiro)**

**Unesp (São Paulo State University)**

**UFMG (Federal University of Minas Gerais)**

**PUC-Rio (Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro)**

**UFRGS (Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul)**

**UFSC (Federal University of Santa Catarina)**

**UnB (University of Brasília)**

**Unifesp (Federal University of São Paulo)**

**What Changes Compared to THE:** the **QS** traditionally **values market perception more** (employability) and global connections.

Therefore, institutions with a **strong brand** among employers and **active exchanges** tend to **gain positions**.

## How Rankings Measure “Quality” — and What You Should Observe

Both rankings evaluate **teaching, research, and impact**, but **with different weights**. In practical terms:

**THE**: favors **bibliometric metrics** (normalized citations by field), **learning environment**, and **partnerships**. If you are looking for **graduate studies** and **high-impact research**, performance in THE is a **good thermometer**.

**QS**: gives greater visibility to **reputation** (academic and among employers) and **internationalization** (foreign students/faculty, global networks). If your focus is on **employability** and **international networks**, reading the QS is **strategic**.

**Practical Tip:** when comparing the **best universities in Brazil**, combine the Top 10 from THE and QS with **specific indicators for your course** (program grades, departmental output, laboratories, internship agreements).

**A university strong overall may have variations by area**, so it is worth looking at the **discipline ranking**.

## USP and Unicamp: Consistent Leadership

![unicamp](https://clickpetroleoegas.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/A-lista-completa-das-10-melhores-universidades-do-Brasil-em-2025-segundo-os-rankings-THE-e-QS-1-1095x730.jpg)UNICAMP

**USP** and **Unicamp** appear at the **national leadership** in both rankings.

This is not by chance: both sustain **high research volume**, **good citation rates**, **academic reputation**, and **interaction with the productive sector**.

The **USP**, in particular, has **scale**, diversity of areas, and **international reach**; **Unicamp** stands out for its **scientific intensity per researcher** and **innovation**, with a strong track record of **patents** and **spin-offs**.

For those aiming for **master’s/doctorate** or careers in **R&D**, this **dual performance** indicates **robust** environments, with **leading advisors** and **competitive infrastructure**.

## Federal Institutions on the Rise and the Role of Excellent Private Institutions

The group of federal universities — **UFRJ, UFMG, UFRGS, UFSC, Unifesp, UFSCar, UnB** — forms the **backbone** of Brazilian science, with **university hospitals**, **technology parks**, and centers of **excellence** in various fields.

**PUC-Rio** is the recurring standout private institution, much due to its combination of **qualified research**, **international partnerships**, and **employability** of graduates.

**Advice for Candidates:** if you want an **academic career**, federal universities offer **broad research ecosystems**; if you are looking for **market insertion** with **international traffic**, excellent private institutions like **PUC-Rio** can accelerate connections and opportunities.

## Costs, Scholarships, and Returns: Is It Worth Focusing Only on the Top 10?

Not necessarily. Being among the **best universities in Brazil** helps — **networking**, **laboratories**, and **recognized brands** matter.

But **course, guidance, and internships** weigh as much as the institution’s “name.” Three filters help in decision-making:

**Course Project**: updated curriculum, **practical load**, laboratories, and **partnerships**.

**Career Path**: history of **internships**, **employability** of the course, and **alumni** working where you want to go.

**Cost and Scholarship**: federal universities offer **free education**; top private universities require **planning** (scholarships, financial aid, merit). **Return** depends on the **field** and the **quality of your trajectory**.

## How to Read the 2025 Results Without Falling into “Rankingitis”

Use the **THE** to compare **research and teaching** from a global perspective.

Use the **QS** to assess **reputation and internationalization**.

Cross-reference with **indicators by area** (engineering, health, computing, humanities, etc.).

Prioritize **the best course for you** within the **best universities in Brazil** — not the other way around.

Between **THE** and **QS**, the message for 2025 is clear: the [**best universities in Brazil** remain **competitive**](https://clickpetroleoegas.com.br/brasileiros-descobrem-no-registrato-banco-central-que-dividas-antigas-chaves-pix-e-contas-esquecidas-podem-causar-credito-negado-em-todo-o-brasil-btl96/) in the Latin American scenario thanks to the **strength of public research** and the **quality of some excellent private institutions**.

Now, we want to hear from those who live this experience:

==**For you, what matters most in the choice — reputation, laboratory, employability, internationalization, or scholarship?** And does your course stand out within your university? **Tell us in the comments** how you are deciding, and what else is missing in the rankings to reflect the **reality of Brazilian students**.==

# Study in Brazil

Perhaps best-known for its sport and breathtaking scenery, Brazil is home to more than 2,500 universities, with elite institutions including the University of São Paulo, the biggest public university in the country and one of the best in Latin America. Also home to São Paulo State University, Brazil’s largest city and financial capital is also considered the nation’s cultural centre, home to a plethora of museums, art galleries and concert halls - and it has a vibrant nightlife.

Brazil’s 8,000km of coastline include thousands of spectacular beaches. Also unmissable is carnival season, which starts in February. Rio de Janeiro’s carnival is the biggest in the world, with more than two million people lining the streets each day to witness more than 300 bands and samba schools.

Brazil produces a third of the world’s coffee and is renowned for a wide variety of street food. The country's football team has won the World Cup more than any other nation, and football, by far the most popular sport, has been likened to a religion in the country. But many also like volleyball and, to a slightly lesser extent, mixed martial arts and basketball. Famous Brazilians include footballer Pelé and the late Formula 1 racing driver Ayrton Senna.

Public universities have free tuition for home and international students, but places are limited and most students attend private institutions.

For broader coverage of this topic, see [Universities and Higher Education in Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universities_and_Higher_Education_in_Brazil "Universities and Higher Education in Brazil").

Universities in [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil") are ranked in a number of ways, including both national and international ranks.

## National Rankings

### Ranking Universitário Folha

Since 2012, Brazil's largest newspaper [Folha de S. Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folha_de_S._Paulo "Folha de S. Paulo") has organized a national ranking of universities[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rankings_of_universities_in_Brazil#cite_note-RUF-1) with criteria akin to those used by better known worldwide rankings: research, teaching, internationalization, innovation and market value.

### Brazilian government evaluation

Higher education evaluations are also conducted by the Brazilian Government; specifically by **Inep** (Instituto Nacional de Estudos e
Pesquisas Educacionais; English: National Institute of Studies and Research). The Government uses a **General Index of Courses** (Portuguese: [Índice Geral de Cursos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Índice_Geral_de_Cursos?action=edit&redlink=1 "Índice Geral de Cursos (page does not exist)") [[pt](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Índice%20Geral%20de%20Cursos "pt:Índice Geral de Cursos")]; **IGC**) to determine the quality of Brazilian's higher education (graduate and post-graduate courses) in [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"). [Universidade de São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universidade_de_São_Paulo "Universidade de São Paulo"), one of the most prestigious universities in the country, has been participating in the **IGC** since 2013 as part of a technical cooperation with **Inep** that will last three years, during which time the results concerning the university's courses will not be disclosed. Only then will the university decide whether to fully participate in the government evaluation.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rankings_of_universities_in_Brazil#cite_note-RUF-1)

# Latin America University Rankings 2022: results announced

### [**Browse the Latin America University Rankings 2022 results**](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/2022/latin-america-university-rankings#!/page/0/length/25/sort_by/rank/sort_order/asc/cols/undefined)

---

Brazilian universities are the best-performing institutions in Latin America, on average, according to *Times Higher Education*’s latest ranking for the region.

Brazil has the highest average overall score of all countries of 51.3 out of 100, up from 48.9 last year, based on nations with 10 or more universities ranked this year and last. The country dominates the top of the *THE* Latin America University Rankings, with 28 universities in the top 50 and seven in the top 10.

However, the top spot goes to a Chilean university, [Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/pontificia-universidad-catolica-de-chile), for the fourth year in a row.

The second and third spots are both taken by Brazilian institutions: the [University of São Paulo](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/university-sao-paulo) and the [University of Campinas](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/university-campinas). Both scored the highest possible marks for research, and also scored well for teaching.

The countries with the most ranked institutions are Brazil with 72 universities, followed by Chile (30), Colombia (29), Mexico (26), Ecuador (13) and Peru (10).

Brazil also has the highest average score for teaching, at 55.6, while Mexico is second with 43.5 and Chile third at 35.9. Brazil has the highest average score for research, too.

---

*[Latin America University Rankings 2022 digital edition](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/digital-editions/latin-america-university-rankings-2022-digital-edition)  
[Latin American higher education beyond the pandemic](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/opinion/latin-america-university-rankings-2022-he-beyond-pandemic)  
[New shoots emerge in a challenging region](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/latin-america-university-rankings-2022-new-shoots-emerge-challenging)*  

---

Antonio José de Almeida Meirelles, rector of the University of Campinas, attributed its success in part to the funding model in the state of São Paulo, which it says has enabled the institution to plan long-term.

“There is a legal provision in force in São Paulo that obliges the state to allocate, every year, the same percentage of the revenue of its main tax – the so-called ICMS – to fund the activities of Unicamp [and other state universities]…The creation of this provision, in 1989, has made it possible for the São Paulo state universities to plan their investments ahead and strategically over the last three decades,” Meirelles said.

He added: “Currently, the existence of this mechanism is helping to keep Unicamp and its sisters relatively protected from the harmful effects of the cuts in federal funds for science and technology, which contributes to them doing well in the rankings.”

He also attributed the success to high-quality processes for selecting academics, staff and undergraduate and postgraduate students.

The *THE* Latin America University Rankings lists the top institutions in the Latin America and Caribbean region. It is based on the same 13 rigorous performance indicators that underpin the [*THE* World University Rankings](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/2022#!/page/0/length/25/sort_by/rank/sort_order/asc/cols/stats), but the [weightings have been recalibrated to reflect the characteristics of Latin America’s universities](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/latin-america-university-rankings-2022-methodology). Universities are evaluated across all their core missions: teaching, research, knowledge transfer and international outlook.

The 2022 ranking includes 197 institutions across 13 countries, up from 177 institutions last year.

# These Are The 5 Best Universities In Brazil Right Now

Defining which are the **5 best universities in Brazil** is a task that mobilizes students and the market annually. For 2025, the main university rankings indicate a consolidated leadership of the University of São Paulo (USP), but show a fierce competition for a place on the podium, which continues to reflect the excellence of research and education in the country.

An analysis of the results of the most important global and national rankings reveals which institutions stand out. The list is dominated by public universities, which, despite budgetary challenges, continue to be the reference in knowledge production and academic excellence in the country. Better and more reliable options than seeking shortcuts, such as [buying a diploma](https://diplomarapido.com.br/).

## The Consolidated Podium: Who Are the **5 Best Universities** in Brazil?

Based on the compilation of results from the QS World University, Times Higher Education (THE), and Folha University Ranking (RUF), the list of the **5 best universities in Brazil** has consolidated as follows:

1. **University of São Paulo (USP)**
2. **State University of Campinas (Unicamp)**
3. **Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ)**
4. **São Paulo State University (Unesp)**
5. **Federal University of Minas Gerais (UFMG)**

It is important to note that the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS) also stands out, frequently alternating with UFMG and Unesp in the competition for positions in the top 5, depending on the methodology of each ranking.

## Performance in the QS World University Rankings 2025

Published in **June 2024** by the British consultancy Quacquarelli Symonds, the QS World University Rankings is one of the most influential in the world. In the 2025 edition, **USP was the main Brazilian highlight, reaching the 92nd global position**, placing it among the 100 best institutions on the planet.

The ranking of other Brazilian universities in the top 5, according to QS, was:

- **Unicamp:** 232nd global position.
- **UFRJ:** 304th global position.
- **Unesp:** 489th global position.
- **UFMG:** Range 601-610 global.

## The Evaluation of Times Higher Education (THE) 2025

The ranking from the British magazine Times Higher Education, published in **October 2024**, uses a methodology with 18 indicators, focused on teaching, research, and international perspective. In it, USP’s leadership is also confirmed.

The ranking of Brazilian institutions in the top 5, according to THE, was:

- **USP:** Range 201-250 global.
- **Unicamp:** Range 351-400 global.
- **UFRJ:** Range 501-600 global.
- **Unesp:** Range 601-800 global.
- **UFRGS:** Range 601-800 global.

In this evaluation, UFRGS appears in fifth place, tied with Unesp, demonstrating the competitiveness among federal institutions.

## The National Perspective: What Does the Folha University Ranking (RUF) Say?

The RUF, promoted by the newspaper Folha de S.Paulo, is the most comprehensive and detailed evaluation of Brazilian universities. Its last complete edition was published in **November 2023**, and its results reinforce the scenario seen in international rankings.

The top 5 of RUF 2023 was:

1. **University of São Paulo (USP)**
2. **State University of Campinas (Unicamp)**
3. **Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ)**
4. **Federal University of Minas Gerais (UFMG)**
5. **Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS)**

## What Defines Excellence? The Strength of Research and Education

The analysis of the three main rankings shows that, despite different methodologies, the same group of public universities consistently remains at the top. The absolute leadership of USP, closely followed by Unicamp and UFRJ, is a consolidated fact.

The strength of these institutions lies in their **intense scientific production, the high qualification of their professors, and the impact of their research** on society. These are the pillars that guarantee them the status of the **5 best universities in Brazil** and [position them as excellence references](https://clickpetroleoegas.com.br/qual-foi-o-primeiro-ensino-medio-no-brasil-btl96/) in Latin America.

# [2403.18140] Juru: Legal Brazilian Large Language Model from Reputable Sources

[View PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.18140) [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2)
> Abstract:The high compute cost associated with pretraining large language models limits their research. Two strategies have emerged to address this issue: domain specialization and pretraining with high-quality data. To explore these strategies, we specialized the Mistral-7B model with 1.9 billion unique tokens from reputable Brazilian legal sources and conducted few-shot evaluations on legal and general knowledge test suites. Our model, Juru, demonstrates the benefits of domain specialization by achieving improved performance on legal benchmarks, even with a reduced amount of pretraining data. However, this domain specialization through continued pretraining comes at the cost of increased forgetting in unrelated domains, as evidenced by performance degradation on general knowledge test suites in both Portuguese and English. This study contributes to the growing body of scientific evidence showing that pretraining data selection may enhance the performance of large language models, enabling the exploration of these models at a lower cost. Juru is publicly available at [this https URL](https://huggingface.co/roseval/Juru-7B) .

# Juru: Legal Brazilian Large Language Model from Reputable Sources

Roseval Malaquias Junior Affiliation: Computer Science Department, University of São Paulo, São Carlos, São Paulo, Brazil  
, E-mail <roseval@usp.br> Affiliation: Maritaca AI, Campinas, São Paulo, Brazil E-mail [{ramon, rodrigo}@maritaca.ai](mailto:%7Bramon,%20rodrigo%7D@maritaca.ai) Ramon Pires Roseli A. F. Romero Affiliation: Computer Science Department, University of São Paulo, São Carlos, São Paulo, Brazil  
, E-mail <roseval@usp.br> Rodrigo Nogueira E-mail <rafrance@icmc.usp.br> Affiliation: Maritaca AI, Campinas, São Paulo, Brazil E-mail [{ramon, rodrigo}@maritaca.ai](mailto:%7Bramon,%20rodrigo%7D@maritaca.ai)

###### Abstract

The high compute cost associated with pretraining large language models limits their research. Two strategies have emerged to address this issue: domain specialization and pretraining with high-quality data. To explore these strategies, we specialized the Mistral-7B model with 1.9 billion unique tokens from reputable Brazilian legal sources and conducted few-shot evaluations on legal and general knowledge test suites. Our model, Juru, demonstrates the benefits of domain specialization by achieving improved performance on legal benchmarks, even with a reduced amount of pretraining data. However, this domain specialization through continued pretraining comes at the cost of increased forgetting in unrelated domains, as evidenced by performance degradation on general knowledge test suites in both Portuguese and English. This study contributes to the growing body of scientific evidence showing that pretraining data selection may enhance the performance of large language models, enabling the exploration of these models at a lower cost. Juru is publicly available at <https://huggingface.co/roseval/Juru-7B>.

###### Keywords:

Domain Specialization Continued Pretraining Legal Language Models Low-Resource Pretraining

## 1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) are commonly trained on vast amounts of general-purpose data sourced from internet snapshots, such as the CommonCrawl [[3](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib3 ""), [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib4 ""), [32](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib32 "")] and C4 [[32](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib32 ""), [34](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib34 "")]. Scaling laws [[14](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib14 "")] support this paradigm, suggesting more capable models with increased data and trainable parameters. As a result, LLMs developed through this method demonstrate the ability to address tasks across multiple languages and domains [[20](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib20 "")].

The significant computational resources required for pretraining with such massive datasets pose a challenge for research, limiting the exploration of their capabilities. However, it is possible to observe competitive results on a smaller scale through the application of continued pretraining.
In the literature, the selection of domain-specific data [[8](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib8 ""), [9](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib9 ""), [22](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib22 "")] from reputable sources [[12](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib12 ""), [18](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib18 ""), [21](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib21 "")] stands out.

The large general-purpose pretraining of LLMs promotes general factual knowledge and language comprehension. Therefore, continued pretraining on the same scale and scope might not be necessary to improve LLMs’ performance.
By employing domain-specific data from reputable sources, we postulate that an LLM initially trained on general-purpose data can improve its performance in a specific domain with minimal additional data, although this may come at the expense of performance degradation in other domains.

To test this hypothesis, we specialized the Mistral-7B [[15](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib15 "")] model for the Brazilian legal domain, using <!-- MathML: <math alttext="1.9" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S1.p4.m1"><semantics><mn>1.9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.9</annotation></semantics></math> --> 1.91.9 billion unique tokens sourced mainly from academic studies from reputable sources. The resulting model, Juru, was evaluated on multiple-choice test suites covering both Brazilian legal knowledge and general knowledge domains. Our objective is to assess the impact of incorporating exclusively domain-specific data during continued pretraining on the model’s performance.

Across the proposed pretraining, our model demonstrated enhanced performance on the legal test suite, while exhibiting a decrease in performance on the general knowledge test suites. In particular, a more pronounced decrease was observed on the English test suite compared to the Portuguese one, suggesting that previously acquired knowledge is better retained when it shares greater similarity with the target domain of specialization. These results contribute to the growing body of scientific evidence supporting the effectiveness of specialized pretraining for improving the performance of generalist models on specific domains. Such specialization may facilitate their research by reducing the compute cost associated with training. Additionally, the resulting model, Juru, is publicly released to support further research on domain specialization through continued pretraining. To the best of our knowledge, Juru is the first LLM pretrained for the Brazilian legal domain.

## 2 Related Work

The increasing scale of LLMs, in both parameter numbers and training data, has led to the emergence of previously unseen abilities in smaller-scale models [[33](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib33 "")]. Recent advances have enabled these models to achieve human-level performance across various tasks that require textual comprehension, specialized knowledge, mathematical reasoning, multilingualism, programming, and image interpretation [[20](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib20 "")]. With such results, it is arguable that these models demonstrate the capacity to integrate these diverse skills in a cohesive manner.

Language and domain specialization have become effective strategies for ensuring that LLMs bring tangible benefits in real-world applications. Recent works have shown that continued pretrained in language-specific corpora, particularly in Portuguese [[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib1 ""), [17](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib17 ""), [22](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib22 "")], enhances significantly the performance of downstream tasks without the need to increase the parameter count.

The Brazilian legal field emerges as a relevant example of such domain specialization, as previous studies have underscored the performance of language models pretrained on legal corpora [[9](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib9 ""), [24](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib24 "")].
However, those models are encoder-only, lacking the ability to generate text sequentially, which is essential for several legal applications.

SaulLM-7B [[8](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib8 "")] is the first LLM pretrained to tackle the nuances of legal languages and follow instructions to support conversation interactions. Starting from Mistral-7B [[15](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib15 "")], the model was pretrained on 30 billion tokens of an English legal dataset. In a subsequent study, Colombo et al. [[7](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib7 "")] scaled this approach to a Mixture-of-Experts architecture. The authors continually pretrained Mixtral-54B and Mixtral-141B on 540 billion tokens of English legal texts, producing SaulLM-54B and SaulLM-141B. While these larger models achieve higher performance on most in-domain tasks, their increased size correlates with lower performance on certain legal tasks.

To the best of our knowledge, Juru is the first LLM pretrained for the Brazilian legal domain. Our experiments show that, relative to its base model, Juru achieves superior performance on in-domain tasks. However, its performance deteriorates on tasks beyond the Brazilian legal domain.

## 3 Methodology

In this section, we describe the gathering and curation of data from public sources within the Brazilian legal domain, as well as the pretraining of the Juru model, including its base model, hyperparameters, and optimization methods.

### 3.1 Pretraining Data

We conducted web scraping of academic papers in Portuguese within the Brazilian legal domain, prioritizing data with educational value.

Academic papers were scraped from various reputable sources that catalog research from Brazilian higher education institutions and national journals. Each platform offers filters for extracting Brazilian papers exclusively in Portuguese, accessible for non-commercial distribution. Also, we scraped the LexML11 1 [https://www.lexml.gov.br](https://www.lexml.gov.br/ "") database, focusing on a subset of Brazilian federal laws.

A total of 13,278 documents were extracted from academic paper databases. Nearly <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" display="inline" alttext="99\%" id="S3.SS1.p3.m1"><semantics><mrow><mn>99</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">99\%</annotation></semantics></math> --> 99%99\% of these documents are in Portable Document Format (PDF). Hence, we used Marker22 2 <https://github.com/VikParuchuri/marker> for extracting text from these documents.

Texts from 14,743 federal laws were extracted from the LexML database. Additionally, the dataset from the study by Sakiyama et al. [[27](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib27 "")] was added to the pretraining dataset, consisting of 32,535 legal documents distributed between decisions and judgments from the Brazilian Supreme Federal Court.

After extracting the documents, they were automatically curated using the filter proposed by Rae et al. [[25](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib25 "")], adapted for Portuguese. This filter removes documents that are unlikely to be predominantly natural language, such as tables or long lists, as they could hinder the learning process of the LLM.

Table 1: Distribution of Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) [[29](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib29 "")] tokens for the pretraining dataset, using the Mistral-7B tokenizer.

Considering the tokenizer of Mistral-7B, the model employed in our pretraining, we gathered <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="1.9" id="S3.SS1.p6.m1"><semantics><mn>1.9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.9</annotation></semantics></math> --> 1.91.9 billion tokens, as shown in Table [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Pretraining Data ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Juru: Legal Brazilian Large Language Model from Reputable Sources"). Each document was divided into sequences of 4,096 tokens.

### 3.2 Juru Model

The Juru model extends the causal language modeling pretraining of a Mistral-7B model, without instruction finetuning. We employed the t5x and seqio frameworks [[26](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib26 "")] for the proposed pretraining.

Although more recent models [[10](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib10 ""), [11](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib11 "")] of comparable size have demonstrated superior performance compared to Mistral-7B, we chose Mistral-7B due to its earlier release date. This decision aims to reduce the risk of data contamination in our test suites.

For the pretraining hyperparameters, we employed the AdaFactor optimizer [[30](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib30 "")] without factorization, with a first-order momentum of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="0.9" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S3.SS2.p3.m1"><semantics><mn>0.9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.9</annotation></semantics></math> --> 0.90.9 and a second-order momentum of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="1-k^{-0.8}" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S3.SS2.p3.m2"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.8</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-k^{-0.8}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 1−k−0.81-k^{-0.8}, where <!-- MathML: <math alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S3.SS2.p3.m3"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> --> kk represents the current training step. Additionally, we applied dynamic weight decay by <!-- MathML: <math alttext="lr^{2}" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S3.SS2.p3.m4"><semantics><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">lr^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> --> l​r2lr^{2}, with <!-- MathML: <math alttext="lr" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S3.SS2.p3.m5"><semantics><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">lr</annotation></semantics></math> --> l​rlr as the current learning rate value, and global norm clipping of <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="1.0" id="S3.SS2.p3.m6"><semantics><mn>1.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0</annotation></semantics></math> --> 1.01.0.

In addition to the loss associated with the causal language modeling task, we used an auxiliary loss of <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" display="inline" alttext="10^{-4}\log^{2}\left(\sum_{i}e^{z_{i}}\right)" id="S3.SS2.p4.m1"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msup><mi>log</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0em">∑</mo><mi>i</mi></msub><msup><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-4}\log^{2}\left(\sum_{i}e^{z_{i}}\right)</annotation></semantics></math> --> 10−4​log2⁡(∑iezi)10^{-4}\log^{2}\left(\sum_{i}e^{z_{i}}\right), where <!-- MathML: <math alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S3.SS2.p4.m2"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> --> zz denotes the logits of the prediction. This auxiliary loss helps dampen the values of the pretraining loss. The learning rate is initially set at <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="0" id="S3.SS2.p4.m3"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> --> 00 and gradually increases during a linear warm-up period of <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" display="inline" alttext="250" id="S3.SS2.p4.m4"><semantics><mn>250</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">250</annotation></semantics></math> --> 250250 training steps until it reaches <!-- MathML: <math alttext="0.001" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S3.SS2.p4.m5"><semantics><mn>0.001</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.001</annotation></semantics></math> --> 0.0010.001. Following this warm-up phase, the learning rate remains constant.

The model was pretrained for causal language modeling on a cluster of TPUs v2-256. Each batch consisted of 512 sequences, with 4,096 tokens in each sequence. Training was conducted for 3,800 steps, corresponding to approximately 4 epochs, processing a total of 7.96 billion tokens. The entire pretraining consumed <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" display="inline" alttext="3.35\times 10^{20}\,\text{FLOPs}" id="S3.SS2.p5.m1"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>3.35</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>20</mn></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>FLOPs</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.35\times 10^{20}\,\text{FLOPs}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 3.35×1020​FLOPs3.35\times 10^{20}\,\text{FLOPs} of compute [[16](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib16 "")], taking <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" display="inline" alttext="30.61" id="S3.SS2.p5.m2"><semantics><mn>30.61</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30.61</annotation></semantics></math> --> 30.6130.61 hours to complete. ## 4 Evaluation

Evaluating LLMs for text generation poses challenges due to the subjective nature of emerging skills such as natural language understanding and domain expertise, alongside their ability to integrate these skills for problem-solving. Given their broad capabilities, evaluating with open-ended questioning provides insights into the models’ knowledge representation and their capacity to generate human-like responses [[35](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib35 "")].

However, the evaluation of responses to open-ended questions poses inherent difficulties. Human evaluation is resource-intensive, requiring expertise in specific domain tasks and training in evaluation methodology for experimental robustness. Additionally, relying solely on SOTA LLMs for evaluation may yield a low correlation with human judges due to specific vocabulary and knowledge of a target domain. Hence, there’s an increasing emphasis on evaluating these models using standardized multiple-choice exams, such as those used in university admission processes [[2](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib2 ""), [5](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib5 ""), [19](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib19 ""), [23](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib23 ""), [28](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib28 "")]. Such exams cover diverse topics and skills, proving advantageous for LLM evaluation.

We investigate how continued pretraining through domain specialization influences both knowledge learning and forgetting. Hence, we evaluate the specialized Juru model on three standardized multiple-choice test suites: Brazilian legal knowledge, representing the target domain of our specialization; Portuguese general knowledge, which share the same language as the target domain but do not assess legal knowledge; and English general knowledge, whose distribution is closer to the original English-centric training data of Mistral-7B.

For all test suites, we adopt accuracy as the primary evaluation metric. We group all editions of the same exam administered within a given year into a single evaluation group. When aggregating multiple exams, we report the mean accuracy. Lastly, we employ few-shot learning with three examples during our evaluation, as the model was trained solely for text completion and did not undergo any instruction finetuning.

### 4.1 Brazilian Legal Knowledge

For evaluating the Juru model, we used questions from six Bar Association Exams (OAB) of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="2024" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.p1.m1"><semantics><mn>2024</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2024</annotation></semantics></math> --> 20242024 and <!-- MathML: <math alttext="2023" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S4.SS1.p1.m2"><semantics><mn>2023</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2023</annotation></semantics></math> --> 20232023, and two National Judiciary Exams (ENAM) of <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" alttext="2024" intent=":literal" id="S4.SS1.p1.m3"><semantics><mn>2024</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2024</annotation></semantics></math> --> 20242024. The OAB exam is mandatory for all law graduates aspiring to practice law in Brazil. It comprises two phases; the initial phase encompasses <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="80" id="S4.SS1.p1.m4"><semantics><mn>80</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">80</annotation></semantics></math> --> 8080 multiple-choice questions, while the second phase consists of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S4.SS1.p1.m5"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math> --> 44 essay questions and the creation of a procedural document. ENAM was introduced in 2023 to unify the selection process for entry into the Brazilian judiciary. As of its implementation, only candidates who have passed the ENAM within the last two years are eligible to apply for judicial positions in Brazil. This exam includes a single phase with <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" display="inline" alttext="80" id="S4.SS1.p1.m6"><semantics><mn>80</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">80</annotation></semantics></math> --> 8080 multiple-choice questions. We included only multiple-choice questions from the <!-- MathML: <math alttext="2023" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S4.SS1.p1.m7"><semantics><mn>2023</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2023</annotation></semantics></math> --> 20232023 and <!-- MathML: <math alttext="2024" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S4.SS1.p1.m8"><semantics><mn>2024</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2024</annotation></semantics></math> --> 20242024 OAB, and <!-- MathML: <math alttext="2024" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S4.SS1.p1.m9"><semantics><mn>2024</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2024</annotation></semantics></math> --> 20242024 ENAM exams, comprising a total set of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="638" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.p1.m10"><semantics><mn>638</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">638</annotation></semantics></math> --> 638638 questions, as illustrated in Table [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Brazilian Legal Knowledge ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Juru: Legal Brazilian Large Language Model from Reputable Sources").

### 4.2 Portuguese General Knowledge

Pires et al. [[22](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib22 "")] observed a performance degradation on English benchmarks following the specialization of an English-centric LLM for Portuguese. These results raise the following question: Is catastrophic forgetting limited to cross-linguistic domain specialization, or does specializing in a specific domain within a single language also lead to forgetting of general knowledge in that language?

To address this question, we examined the impact of specializing the Juru model in the Brazilian legal domain on its performance in Portuguese general knowledge tasks, using the multiple-choice exams listed in Table [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Portuguese General Knowledge ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Juru: Legal Brazilian Large Language Model from Reputable Sources"), comprising a total amount of 2,123 questions.

Table 3: Configuration of Portuguese general knowledge test suite.

Following Almeida et al. [[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib1 "")], we ignore all the questions that require image understanding. Some exams have captions describing the image contents. In those cases, we incorporate them into the exact position the images would appear.

### 4.3 English General Knowledge

Unlike the Sabiá [[22](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib22 "")] model, which underwent extensive continued pretraining, the Juru model was trained for fewer steps due to the smaller size of its legal specialization dataset. While Pires et al. [[22](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib22 "")] observed a loss of English knowledge in their model after extended training on Portuguese data, their experiments involved a significantly longer training regime and a more diverse dataset. This raises another question: Can shorter, domain-specific pretraining mitigate or prevent catastrophic forgetting of previously learned knowledge?

To investigate this, we evaluated the Juru model on the MMLU benchmark [[13](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib13 "")], a widely used test suite for assessing general knowledge and reasoning abilities in English [[15](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib15 ""), [20](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib20 ""), [31](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#bib.bib31 "")]. While MMLU includes a broad range of subjects, such as STEM, humanities, law, and medicine, we restricted our evaluation to the college-level and high school-level subsets, amounting to 4,369 questions, as outlined in Table [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.18140v2#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.3 English General Knowledge ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Juru: Legal Brazilian Large Language Model from Reputable Sources").
